d: (of animals or plants) having stiff coarse hairs or bristles
r: Latin hispidus “rough, hairy, bristly”
s: The hispid hare inhabits forested areas.
old_f: (of animals or plants) having a loud hissing call or rustle
(of animals or plants) native to Spain and the Mediterranean
(of animals or plants) having a smooth and glossy surface
ety: From Latin hispidus (“rough, hairy, bristly”).

d: Not growing or changing; without force or vitality
r: Latin moribundus “dying”
s: These moribund shapes were free as air—and nearly as thin.
old_f: Gloomy and sullen; given to brooding in silence
Strictly moral; bound by rigid rules of conduct
Soft and spongy; easily crushed by the hand
ety: From Latin moribundus (“dying”).

d: An expression introduced into one language by translating it from another language
r: French calque “copy, tracing”, from calquer “to copy, trace”
s: One of the primary benefits of calque is its ability to enhance cross-cultural communication.
old_f: A white powder made by burning and grinding seashells or limestone
A sealing material pressed into the seams of a wooden ship
A brimless cap worn by scholars at an ancient university
ety: From French calque (“calque”, literally “copy, tracing”), from calquer (“to copy, trace”) (whence also calk), itself borrowed from Italian calcare, from Latin calcāre (“to tread”). Doublet of calcate and calcation.

d: A chamber that is used as a grave
r: Latin sepulchrum “grave, burial place”
s: I parked Bertha in a convenient cab rank and raced into the smoked glass sepulchre that is Hanover airport.
old_f: A soft pastry that is filled with cream
A small book that is used for prayer
A clear soup that is served cold
ety: From Middle English sepulchre, sepulcre, sepulker, from late Old English sepulcer, Old French sepulchre, sepulcre, and their etymon Latin sepulchrum, sepulcrum (“grave, burial place”).

d: An archaic word originally meaning ‘in truth’ but now usually used to express disbelief
r: Old English for sōþ “truly, for certain”: for + sooth “truth”
s: A fit man, forsooth, to governe a realme!
old_f: An archaic word originally meaning ‘before noon’ but now usually used for any morning hour
An archaic word originally meaning ‘in the south’ but now usually used in sea songs
An archaic word originally meaning ‘for comfort’ but now usually used to soothe children
ety: From Middle English forsothe, forsoþe, for sothe, from Old English for sōþ (“truly, for certain, forsooth”), equivalent to for (“for, by”) + sooth (“truth”).

d: The property of being close together
r: Latin propinquitās, from propinquus “neighbouring”, from prope “near”
s: Propinquity and corruption don't always go side by side.
old_f: The property of being fitting or proper
The property of being likely to happen
The property of being owned by someone
ety: From propinqu(ent) + -ity, from Middle English propinquite, from Middle French propinquité or Latin propinquitās, from propinquus (“neighbouring”) (from prop(e) (“near”) + (h)inc (“hence”) + -uus).

d: A tangible symbol signifying approval or distinction
r: French accolade, from Occitan acolada “an embrace”, from Latin ad- + collum “neck”
s: The scientist received the highest accolade in her field for the groundbreaking discovery.
old_f: A sweet drink made from crushed lemons
A sudden outburst of loud complaint
A long row of columns along a street
ety: First use appears c. 1591 in the publications of Thomas Lodge, borrowed from French accolade, from Occitan acolada (“an embrace”), from acolar (“to embrace”), from Italian accollato, via Vulgar Latin *accollō (“to hug around the neck”), from Latin ad- + collum (“neck”) (English collar) + -āta.

d: Young and inexperienced
r: Old English calu “without hair, bald”
s: Those three young men are particularly callow youths.
old_f: Hard and thickened
Pale and sickly
Coldly unfeeling
ety: From Middle English calwe (“(adjective) bald; (noun) bald person”), from Old English calu, caluw (“without hair, bald, callow”), from Proto-West Germanic *kalu, from Proto-Germanic *kalwaz (“bald; bare, naked”), and then either: * from Proto-Indo-European *gol(H)-wo- (“bald; bare, naked”), from *gelH- (“head; naked”); or * from Latin calvus (“bald”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kl̥H- (“bald; naked”). If not borrowed from Latin, Grimm’s law indicates that the Latin word is likely a false cognate, along with Persian کل (kal) and Sanskrit कुल्व (kulvá). cognates * Dutch kaal (“bald”) * G

d: An event or situation that happens at the same time as or in connection with another
r: Latin concomitāns, from concomitor “to accompany”, from con- + comitor, from comes “companion”
s: A major concomitant of the advent of diesel traction has been a vast increase in the amount of electrical equipment needing overhaul.
old_f: A formal agreement that binds two or more parties to share the profits of a venture
A person or official who is sent ahead to prepare lodgings for a traveling court
A soothing medicine that is taken to relieve the symptoms of a cold or fever
ety: First attested 1607; from Middle French concomitant, from Latin concomitāns, the present participle of concomitor (“to accompany”), from con- (“together”) + comitor (“to accompany”), from comes (“companion”).

d: Speak unfavorably about
r: Latin trādūcō “carry over; lead as a spectacle, dishonor”, from trāns + dūcō “to lead”
s: Someone must have traduced Joseph K., for without having done anything wrong he was arrested one fine morning.
old_f: Carry across water
Sell goods abroad
Follow a trail
ety: From Latin trādūcō (“carry over; lead as a spectacle, dishonor”), from trāns + dūcō (“to lead”). Doublet of transduce, from Latin trānsdūcō.

d: Something that precedes and indicates the approach of something or someone
r: Middle English herbergeour, one sent ahead to arrange lodgings, from Old French herbergier “to shelter”
s: I knew by these harbingers who were coming.
old_f: Something that shelters a ship from the force of waves or storms
Someone who plays a stringed instrument at a royal court or feast
Something that stores grain or hay through the long winter months
ety: Originally, a person sent in advance to arrange lodgings. From Middle English herberjour, herbergeour, from Old French herbergeor (French hébergeur), from herbergier (“to set up camp; to shelter; to take shelter”) + -or (suffix forming agent nouns), from Old High German heribergan, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *harjabergu (“army camp, shelter”). Compare German Herberge, Italian albergo, Dutch herberg, English harbor. More at here, bury.

d: A pale and sickly appearance
r: French étiolé, from étioler “to blanch”
s: His etiolation signaled years in prison.
old_f: A formal code of good manners
The study of causes of disease
A gradual wearing away of rock
ety: From French étiolé, past participle of étioler (“to blanch”).

d: Very light rain; stronger than mist but less than a shower
r: Late Middle English misellen “to drizzle”
s: When a gawping Byzantine head bounced past his feet, and a mizzle of blood settled upon him, something changed.
old_f: Very fine sand; softer than grit but coarser than silt
Very weak tea; stronger than water but less than a brew
Very small fish; larger than fry but less than a herring
ety: From Late Middle English misellen (“to drizzle”), cognate with Low German miseln, musseln (“to mizzle”), Dutch miezelen (“to drizzle, rain gently”). Of obscure origin, possibly a frequentative related to the base of mist; or, related to Middle Low German mes (“urine”), Middle Dutch mes, mis (“urine”), both from Old Saxon mehs (“urine”), from Proto-Germanic *mihstuz, *mihstaz, *mihsk- (“urine”), from *mīganą (“to urinate”), from Proto-Indo-European *meiǵʰ-, *omeiǵʰ- (“to urinate”). Compare also English micturate (“to urinate”), Old Frisian mese (“urine”), Low German miegen (“to urinate”), Dutch

d: Marked by quiet and caution and secrecy; taking pains to avoid being observed
r: Latin surrēptīcius “furtive, clandestine”, from surrēpō “to creep along”
s: Sophia listened with the studied air of one for whom, even in these days, a title possessed some surreptitious allurement.
old_f: Marked by sudden repetition and constant return; recurring again and again over a long period
Marked by the purchase of goods and land; acquiring property beyond one’s needs
Marked by a strong sense of the strange and dreamlike; seeming unreal or fantastic
ety: Borrowed from Latin surrēptīcius (“furtive, clandestine”), from surrēpō (“to creep along”).

d: An engine that provided medieval artillery used during sieges; a heavy war engine for hurling large stones and other missiles
r: Old French trebuchet, from trebuchier “to overthrow, topple”
s: Medieval trebuchets are said to have been capable of launching 90-kg projectiles over distances of more than 300 meters.
old_f: A tall wooden tower that sheltered archers during sieges; a moving platform rolled up against the walls of a castle
A long iron spike that held down tents during campaigns; a heavy peg driven into the ground with a mallet
A small brass bell that warned of attacks during sieges; a signal hung on the gate of a walled town
ety: From Old French trebuchet, trebuket et al. (modern trébuchet), from trebuchier (“to overthrow, topple”), from tres- + *buchier, from Old French buc (“trunk of the body”), from Old Frankish *būk (“belly, trunk, torso”), from Proto-Germanic *būkaz (“belly, abdomen, trunk”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰōw- (“to blow, swell”). Cognate with Old High German būh (“belly”), Old English būc (“belly, trunk”). More at bouk.

d: Impossible to measure or compare in value or size or excellence
r: Medieval Latin incommensurabilis: in- + commensurable
s: The side and diagonal of a square are incommensurable with each other.
old_f: Impossible to forgive or excuse in law or in morals or in good conscience
Impossible to share or divide between partners or among heirs
Impossible to tell or report in speech or in writing
ety: From Middle French incommensurable, from Medieval Latin incommensurabilis. Its full etymology is equivalent to that of in- + commensurable.

d: A card game for two players using a reduced pack of 32 cards
r: French piquet
s: They would kick off their shoes and play piquet by candle-light.
old_f: A wooden stake for two horses using a short length of rope
A spicy sauce for cold meats using vinegar and chopped pickles
A small dance for two partners using quick steps in triple time
ety: From French piquet.

d: A windstorm that lifts up clouds of dust or sand
r: Italian scirocco “south-east wind”
s: But come, the board is spread; our silver lamp Is trimm’d, and heeds not the sirocco’s damp.
old_f: A rich sauce made from tomatoes, garlic and olive oil
A small fortress built on a rocky cliff above a harbor
A lively dance performed in pairs at Sicilian weddings
ety: Borrowed from Italian scirocco (“south-east wind”).

d: A (usually canopied) seat for riding on the back of a camel or elephant
r: Hindi haudā, from Arabic hawdaj “litter carried by a camel”
s: They don't ask for palanquins and howdahs.
old_f: A (usually painted) drum for beating time at the front of a procession
A (usually woven) blanket for laying on the back of a horse or mule
A (usually silver) lamp for hanging at the door of a temple or shrine
ety: From Hindi हौदा (haudā), from Arabic هَوْدَج (hawdaj, “litter carried by a camel”) (1774).

d: Bursting into flower
r: A- “in” + bloom “flower”
s: When they returned, Jade's cheeks were abloom, her eyes alight with anticipation.
old_f: Covered in mold
Shrouded in gloom
Echoing with booms
ety: From a- (“in”) + bloom (“flower”).

d: A uniformed doorman
r: French commissionaire, from Latin commissio; a doublet of commissioner
s: People hurried in, nodding to the commissionaire, who still wore a tailcoat and a top hat.
old_f: A traveling salesman
A government inspector
A wedding planner
ety: Borrowed from French commissionaire, from Latin commissio. Doublet of commissioner.

d: Make clear and (more) comprehensible
r: Late Latin ēlūcidō “to lighten, enlighten”, from ex- + lūcidus “bright, clear”
s: Another appendix elucidates the S.E.C.R. headcode system.
old_f: Escape and (cleverly) evade
Raise and (greatly) improve
Draw out and (slowly) lengthen
ety: From Late Latin ēlūcidātus, perfect passive participle of ēlūcidō (“to lighten, enlighten”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from ē(x)- (“out, from”) + lūcidus (“bright, clear, understandable”) + -ō (first conjugation verb-forming suffix), literally “to make light of (something)”, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lewk- (“bright; to see; to shine”). Compare French élucider.

d: The ritual washing of a priest’s hands or of sacred vessels
r: Late Latin ablūtiō “a washing away”, from ab- “away” + lavō “wash”
s: There are now indications that it has caused some Americans to become more spartan when it comes to ablutions.
old_f: The ritual blessing of a newly built church or of its bells
The formal removal of a king from his throne or of his crown
The full pardoning of a sinner’s guilt or of his debts
ety: From Middle English ablucioun (“cleansing of impurities”), from Old French ablution, and its source, Late Latin ablūtiō (“a washing away”), from abluō (“wash away”), from ab- (“away”) + lavō (“wash”).

d: The deliberate act of delaying and playing instead of working
r: Middle English daliaunce, from dalien “to exchange pleasantries, to chat; to flirt”; dally + -ance
s: He had passed the officer now. There was no necessity for dalliance.
old_f: The formal act of joining two families by a marriage contract
The careful act of measuring and recording rainfall each day
The steady act of clearing weeds from a flower garden
ety: From Middle English daliaunce et al., from dalien (“to exchange pleasantries, to chat; to flirt”), from Old French dalier, dailer. By surface analysis, dally + -ance.

d: A person of refined upbringing and manners
r: Latin patricius, from patrēs cōnscrīptī “Roman senators”
s: The emperor elevated several loyal families to the status of patricians.
old_f: A person who loves their homeland
A person who supports a family as its head
A person who guards a district at night
ety: Borrowed from Middle French patricien, from Latin patricius, derived from patrēs cōnscrīptī (“Roman senators”). May also have been derived from Latin patricius + -ian

d: Generous in assistance to the poor
r: Medieval Latin eleēmosynārius “alms dispenser”, from Greek eleēmosúnē “alms”
s: Crouch low thy neck to eleemosynary gifts.
old_f: Relating to the basic elements of a subject
Rising sharply in pitch or height
Dressed in fine and fashionable clothes
ety: From Medieval Latin eleēmosynārius (“alms dispenser”), from Late Latin eleēmosyna (“alms”), from Ancient Greek ἐλεημοσύνη (eleēmosúnē, “alms”), from ἐλεήμων (eleḗmōn, “merciful”) + -σῠ́νη (-sŭ́nē, “suffix denoting an abstract noun”). Compare Italian elemosina.

d: Of something having a dusty purplish pink color
r: Anglo-Latin roseātus: rose + -ate
s: The countess took the roseate palm and snowy fingers of this lovely child.
old_f: Of something having a rough and grainy texture
Of something having been turned on a lathe
Of something having the sweet smell of resin
ety: From Middle English roseat, from Anglo-Latin roseātus, equivalent to rose + -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

d: A small gate in the rear of a fort or castle
r: Late Latin posterna and Old French posterne “hidden exit from a fortification”
s: In the outwork was a sally-port corresponding to the postern of the castle, and the whole was surrounded by a strong palisade.
old_f: A tall pole set at the front of a market or fair
A printed notice nailed to the door of a church
A rear guard stationed behind the main body of an army
ety: The noun is derived from Middle English postern, posterne (“side door or gate; small entranceway; hidden or secret door or passage”), from Late Latin posterna, and from its likely etymon Anglo-Norman posterne and Old French posterne (“hidden exit from a fortified building; back door; small door”) (modern French poterne), a variant of posterle (“back door or passage”) (although this is attested later), possibly also influenced by Latin externus (“external, outward”) and internus (“internal, inward”). Posterle is from Late Latin posterla, posterula (“(small) back door, gate, or way”), from Latin

d: Someone who insists on something
r: Middle English stighteler: stickle + -er; judges at Cornish wrestling carry sticks
s: Lexicographers are sticklers for correct language.
old_f: Someone who gathers firewood
Someone who sells adhesive labels
Someone who wins by cheating
ety: From Middle English stighteler, stytelere, equivalent to stickle + -er. The judges at Cornish wrestling matches do indeed carry sticks which serve for signalling and as a badge of their office. This practice has evolved from holding swords and then swordsticks.

d: Barely satisfying a lower standard
r: Hard + scrabble
s: He leads a hardscrabble existence.
old_f: Fond of rough games
Lined with sharp gravel
Stubbornly refusing to bend
ety: From hard + scrabble.

d: Lucky in making unexpected and fortunate discoveries
r: Serendipity + -ous
s: The weather was serendipitous for our vacation.
old_f: Calm and untroubled in manner and spirit
Running in an unbroken series or sequence
Slow to anger and quick to forgive
ety: From serendipity + -ous.

d: Convert to another faith or religion
r: Proselyte + -ize
s: “I am not sent here to proselytize. My church is not in that business.”
old_f: Write in a plain style or manner
Ask for help with great insistence
Speak to a crowd in public
ety: From proselyte + -ize.

d: A natural disposition to be hostile
r: Latin pugnacitas
s: His sister is out front, cleaning her gun with that intimidating pugnacity that has most of the men in town keeping well clear of her.
old_f: A strong smell of rotting leaves
A small flat-faced breed of dog
A stubborn refusal to forgive
ety: From Latin pugnacitas (whence -acity).

d: To make better
r: Late Latin meliorō, from melior “better”
s: They offered some compromises in an effort to meliorate the disagreement.
old_f: Mix together
Make sweeter
Soften with age
ety: First attested in 1542; borrowed from Late Latin meliorātus, perfect passive participle of meliorō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from melior (“better”).

d: A dissolute man in fashionable society
r: Latin prōflīgātus, from prōflīgō “to strike down, cast down”
s: Have you come to Nelson seeking your death, profligate?
old_f: A skilled man in the legal profession
A dashing man of military rank
A learned man of advanced years
ety: The adjective is first attested in 1535, the verb in 1542; borrowed from Latin prōflīgātus, perfect passive participle of prōflīgō (“to strike down, cast down”) (see -ate (etymology 1, 2 an 3) and pro-), from prō- (“forward”) + flīgō (“to strike, dash”) + -ō (1st conjugation compound verb-forming suffix). Common participial usage of the adjective up until Early Modern English.

d: Letter for letter
r: Medieval Latin litterātim, from littera “letter”
s: I shall transcribe its beginning literatim.
old_f: Word by word
In written form
For the record
ety: From Medieval Latin litterātim, from littera (“letter”). First known use: 1643.

d: A trellis on which ornamental shrub or fruit tree is trained to grow flat
r: French espalier, from Italian spalliera, from spalla “shoulder”
s: The great willow pitchforks grown in espalier at villages like Sauve.
old_f: A short sword with which officers of the guard are armed at ceremonies
A thin pastry on which sliced apples are laid in a spiral pattern
A stone bench on which pilgrims rest outside the door of a chapel
ety: Borrowed from French espalier, from Italian spalliera, from spalla (“shoulder”).

d: Political propaganda (especially communist propaganda) communicated via art and literature and cinema
r: Russian agitpróp, short for the Soviet Department for Agitation and Propaganda
s: Like most pieces of agitprop, the Lucas and Sargent paper vastly overstated the deficiencies of the old order.
old_f: Political debate (especially parliamentary debate) conducted through formal speeches and written motions
Theatrical scenery (especially painted scenery) designed to be moved quickly between acts
Stirring music (especially brass band music) played at rallies and military parades
ety: The noun is borrowed from Russian агитпро́п (agitpróp, “agitprop”), Агитпро́п (Agitpróp, “Agitprop (Department for Agitation and Propaganda of the Soviet Union)”), short for отде́л агитации и пропаганды (otdél agitacii i propagandy, “Department for Agitation and Propaganda”); analysable as a blend of agitation + propaganda. The verb is derived from the noun.

d: A name given to a product or service
r: French marque; a doublet of mark
s: The group wants Rover as its luxury marque and MG as the performance car.
old_f: A large tent used for outdoor parties
A nobleman ranking above an earl
A boundary stone marking a frontier
ety: Borrowed from French marque. Doublet of mark. Ultimately cognate with marquee.

d: An explanation or critical interpretation (especially of the Bible)
r: Greek exḗgēsis “interpretation”, from exēgéomai “to explain, interpret”
s: As with Deism and Materialism, the German Rationalism invaded the department of Biblical exegesis.
old_f: A departure or mass migration (especially of a whole people)
A formal ruling or decree (especially of the Pope)
A drawing or plan (especially of a building)
ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐξήγησις (exḗgēsis, “interpretation”), from ἐξηγέομαι (exēgéomai, “to explain, interpret”), from ἐξ (ex, “out”) + ἡγέομαι (hēgéomai, “to lead, guide”).
